chapters.name: Chapter 1: The CHW role and connecting with people

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What community health workers do and how to start
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe the CHW role and find your state's rules for CHWs.
This lesson builds toward: Using national CHW sources and your state's official page, you will describe what a community health worker does and the steps to start in your state, naming at least 3 CHW roles and whether your state certifies CHWs.
The American Public Health Association calls a community health worker a frontline public health worker who is trusted by, or knows the community well. CHWs link people to health and social services and help make care fit people's culture.
The US Bureau of Labor Statistics says CHWs do outreach such as home visits, help coordinate care, link people to transportation, housing and food help, and may do basic health screenings. The National C3 Council lists ten CHW roles, including outreach, health education, care coordination and system navigation, advocacy, and coaching and social support.
A high school diploma is usually the minimum, with on-the-job training. Some states require certification, which may include an approved training program. Check your state's department of health, nursing board or human services department.
This course prepares you. It does not certify you. Employers include community clinics, hospitals, health departments, health plans and nonprofits.
Step by step:
- Search for your state's name plus "community health worker certification".
- Open the result from your state's government site.
- Write whether your state certifies CHWs and what it requires.
- Look at two CHW job posts near you and list the duties.
Words to know:
- Community health worker (CHW): a trusted community member who helps people get health care and other services.
- Promotor or promotora: a common Spanish name for a community health worker.
- Outreach: going to where people are, like homes, events or churches, to share information and offer help.
- Certification: an official record that you met a state's or group's training and test rules.
Official sources:
- APHA: Community Health Workers Section
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Community Health Workers
- National C3 Council: CHW Roles and Competencies
Try it now: Find out whether your state certifies community health workers, using your state's official page. Then find one CHW job post near you. On paper, write your state's rule, three duties from the job post, and one way your own life experience fits the job.
You can now describe what a community health worker does and find your state's rules on an official page.

check.q: Which is a main part of a CHW's job?
options: Linking people to health care and services
check.why: CHWs link people to care and services; clinicians diagnose and prescribe.

check.q: Do all states require CHW certification?
options: No; some states do, so check your state's page
check.why: BLS says some states require certification; rules differ by state.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Listening and plain talk
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use active listening, plain words and teach-back in a practice conversation.
This lesson builds toward: In a practice conversation with a made-up neighbor, you will use active listening, plain language and teach-back, reflecting back what they said and checking they understood, with no jargon.
People share more when they feel heard. Active listening means giving your full attention, letting the person finish, and saying back what you heard: "So getting to the clinic is hard because the bus does not run early. Did I get that right?"
Use plain language. Say "blood sugar" instead of "glucose", and "a paper that shows where you live" instead of "proof of residence". Use short sentences and one idea at a time. Offer an interpreter when someone prefers another language.
Teach-back checks that you explained clearly. Ask the person to say the plan in their own words: "Just so I know I explained it well, can you tell me what you will bring to the food pantry?" If they cannot, the fix is your explanation, not their memory.
Respect means no judging. Ask about what matters to the person and what they already tried. They are the expert on their own life.
Step by step:
- Give full attention and let the person finish.
- Say back what you heard and ask if you got it right.
- Explain the next step in plain words, one idea at a time.
- Use teach-back: ask them to say the plan in their own words.
Words to know:
- Active listening: listening with full attention and saying back what you heard.
- Plain language: short, common words and sentences that are easy to understand.
- Teach-back: asking a person to explain the plan in their own words to check you explained it clearly.
- Jargon: special words a group uses that others may not understand.
Try it now: Role play with a friend or family member, or write it on paper. Your made-up neighbor says: "I keep missing my clinic appointments because I work early and the bus is late." Write a reflect-back sentence, a plain-language next step, and a teach-back question.
You can now listen actively, explain in plain words and check understanding with teach-back.

options: "Can you tell me in your own words what you will bring?"
check.why: Teach-back asks the person to say the plan in their own words.
Common, short words are easiest to understand.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Asking about needs with respect
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask a made-up neighbor about their needs with consent, using a short list.
This lesson builds toward: Using a short list of social needs, you will ask a made-up neighbor about their needs with consent and respect, asking permission first and covering food, housing, transportation, utilities and safety.
Health depends on more than doctor visits. Food, a safe place to live, money for utilities, transportation and safety all affect health. These are often called social needs.
Many clinics and programs use a short screening form. Your employer will give you theirs. The usual topics are: food, housing, utilities, transportation and personal safety.
Always ask permission first and explain why you are asking: "I ask everyone a few questions about things like food and housing, so I can share help that might fit. You can skip any question." Let the person choose what to share.
Write only what you need, on the program's form, not on your own phone. If someone says they are not safe at home, or talks about hurting themselves, follow your program's safety steps right away (see Lesson 6).
Step by step:
- Ask permission and say why you are asking.
- Say they can skip any question.
- Ask about food, housing, utilities, transportation and safety.
- Ask which need matters most to them right now.
- Write only what is needed, on the program's form.
Words to know:
- Social needs: everyday needs like food, housing and transportation that affect health.
- Screening: a short set of questions to find out what help someone may need.
- Consent: permission a person gives after they understand what you are asking.
Try it now: Write a short screening script (practice only): your permission sentence, one plain question each about food, housing, utilities, transportation and safety, and a closing question about what matters most. Read it out loud to check it sounds kind and clear.
You can now ask about someone's needs with consent and respect, using a short list.

check.q: What do you do before asking about someone's needs?
options: Ask permission and say why you are asking
Ask for their Social Security number
Write their answers on your own phone
check.why: Consent and a clear reason build trust before screening.

options: Getting to the clinic when the bus does not run
check.why: Transportation is a social need that affects health.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding and checking local resources
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find a local resource for a need and check it on its official page.
This lesson builds toward: Given a need such as food or a clinic, you will find a local resource and check it on its official page, with the address, phone, hours and how to apply, confirmed on the official page.
A CHW's resource list is only as good as its last check. Programs move, change hours and run out of money. Always check a resource on its own official page or by calling before you refer someone.
Good places to start: call 211, a free, confidential service that connects people with local help. USA.gov's benefits page helps people find government programs for food, housing, health care and utility bills. HRSA's Find a Health Center shows community health centers. HealthCare.gov explains health coverage and how to apply.
For each resource, write down: the name, what it offers, who can use it, the address, phone, hours, how to apply, what to bring, the languages it serves and the date you checked.
If a website is not the official one, find the official page before you trust it. Many fake sites charge fees for forms that are free.
Step by step:
- Name the need, for example food or a clinic.
- Search 211, USA.gov, HRSA's Find a Health Center, or the agency's own site.
- Open the official page and check address, phone, hours and how to apply.
- Write it down with the date you checked.
Words to know:
- Resource: a program or service that helps with a need, like a food pantry or clinic.
- 211: a free, confidential phone service that connects people with local help.
- Community health center: a clinic that serves people whether or not they have insurance.
- Eligibility: the rules about who can use a program.
Official sources:
- 211: Find your local 211
- USA.gov: Government benefits
- HRSA: Find a Health Center
- HealthCare.gov
Try it now: Pick two needs: food and a low-cost clinic. Find one real resource for each near you, check it on its official page, and write the name, address, phone, hours, how to apply and today's date.
You can now find a local resource and check it on its official page before you share it.

check.q: Before you refer someone to a food pantry, what do you do?
options: Check its hours and address on its official page or by phone
Trust a list from three years ago
check.why: Resources change, so check the official page or call first.

check.q: Which service connects people to local help by phone?
options: A random hotline from an ad
check.why: 211 is a free, confidential service that connects people with local help.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making a referral and following up
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a warm referral with consent and a follow-up date.
This lesson builds toward: Given a referral situation, you will plan a referral and a follow-up while keeping privacy and boundaries, with a follow-up date, consent to share, and the right step for a crisis. Given a need such as food or a clinic, you will find a local resource and check it on its official page, with the address, phone, hours and how to apply, confirmed on the official page.
A referral is connecting a person to a service. A "warm" referral means you help make the connection, for example calling the clinic together, instead of only handing over a phone number.
Ask before you share anything about the person: "Is it OK if I tell the clinic you need an evening appointment?" Share only what is needed, and follow your program's consent form.
Help remove barriers. Does the person have a ride, child care, the papers they need, a phone that works? Write what they will bring and when they will go.
Follow up. Set a date to check in: "I'll call you Friday to see how it went." If the service did not work out, find another one. Write the result in the program's record.
Step by step:
- Agree on the need and the service with the person.
- Get consent before sharing any information.
- Make a warm connection, such as a call together.
- Plan for barriers: ride, child care, papers.
- Set and keep a follow-up date, and record the result.
Words to know:
- Referral: connecting a person to a service that can help them.
- Warm referral: helping the person connect directly, such as calling together, not just giving a number.
- Barrier: something that makes it hard to get help, like no ride or no child care.
- Follow-up: checking back later to see if the help worked.
Try it now: Practice only: your made-up neighbor, Ms. Carter, needs food for her two kids and has no car. Using a food resource you checked in Lesson 4, write a warm referral plan: what you will say, the consent question, one barrier and how you will help with it, and a follow-up date.
You can now plan a warm referral with consent, help with barriers and set a follow-up date.

options: Helping them connect, such as calling together
check.why: A warm referral helps the person connect directly.

check.q: You want to tell a clinic about a neighbor's situation. First you:
options: Post it in a group chat
check.why: Consent comes before sharing any information.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Privacy, boundaries, crisis steps and your resource guide
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Keep privacy and boundaries, follow crisis steps, and build your resource guide.
This lesson builds toward: Given a referral situation, you will plan a referral and a follow-up while keeping privacy and boundaries, with a follow-up date, consent to share, and the right step for a crisis. Given a need such as food or a clinic, you will find a local resource and check it on its official page, with the address, phone, hours and how to apply, confirmed on the official page.
People trust you with private things. Health information is protected by a federal law called HIPAA when you work for a clinic, hospital or health plan, and every good program keeps people's information private. Do not talk about the people you serve with friends, post about them or keep notes on your own phone.
Boundaries keep the work healthy. You are a guide, not a doctor, lawyer or bank. Do not give medical or legal advice, lend money or promise what you cannot deliver. Health questions go to clinicians.
Know your crisis steps. If someone is in danger now, call 911. If someone talks about suicide or is in emotional crisis, they can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or chat online. Tell your supervisor right away and follow your program's safety plan.
Take care of yourself too. Helping people with hard lives is heavy work. Talk with your supervisor, take breaks and use your own support. Now you are ready to build your resource guide and referral plan.
Step by step:
- Keep information private: no talk, posts or personal-phone notes.
- Stay in your role: no medical or legal advice, no lending money.
- Crisis: 911 for danger now; 988 for suicide or emotional crisis; tell your supervisor.
- Build your resource guide with at least five checked resources and a referral plan.
Words to know:
- HIPAA: a federal law that protects the privacy of health information held by health care providers and health plans.
- Boundary: a clear limit on what you do in a work relationship.
- 988: the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call, text or chat.
- Self-care: things you do to keep yourself healthy and able to keep helping.
Official sources:
- 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
- MedlinePlus: Patient Rights
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page community resource guide with at least five resources (food, housing, health care, health coverage and one more), each checked on its official page with address, phone, hours, how to apply and the date checked. Then write a referral plan for a made-up neighbor: their need in their words, the resource, what you will say, the consent question, one barrier and a follow-up date.
You can now build a checked resource guide and plan a referral that keeps privacy, boundaries and safety.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Checked resources Fewer than five resources, or details not checked on official pages. At least five resources (food, housing, health care, coverage and one more), each with address, phone, hours, how to apply and the date checked. Also notes who can use each one, what to bring and the languages served. Need in their words The need is a guess or uses jargon. The made-up neighbor's need is written in their own words, with consent noted. Shows which need matters most to them and why. Plain, respectful talk What you will say uses jargon or judges the person. Plain words, a reflect-back sentence and a teach-back question. Offers an interpreter or another way to communicate when needed. Warm referral and follow-up Only a phone number, or no follow-up date. A warm connection, one barrier with a plan, and a follow-up date. Includes a backup resource if the first does not work. Privacy and role Uses a real person's details or gives medical advice. Made-up person, consent before sharing, no medical or legal advice. Lists the crisis steps (911, 988, tell your supervisor) on the guide. Your state path No information on how to become a CHW in your state. Notes whether your state certifies CHWs, with the official page. Adds one local employer or training program to contact. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check it again.

check.q: A person you serve says they are thinking about ending their life. What do you do?
options: Tell them to sleep on it
Connect them to 988 (or 911 if in danger now) and tell your supervisor
check.why: Follow crisis steps: 988 or 911, and tell your supervisor right away.

check.q: A person asks you to lend them $100. What do you do?
options: Kindly say no and help find a resource for the need
check.why: Lending money crosses a boundary; help connect them to a resource instead.
